title: UML for Interviews
summary: The handful of boxes and arrows that let you sketch a class design on a whiteboard in seconds.

blocks.markdown:
**UML (Unified Modeling Language)** is a shared notation for drawing class designs — boxes for classes, arrows for how they relate.

- In an LLD interview it's a **communication tool**, not a spec to memorize.
- A quick class diagram tells the interviewer your design *before* you write code.
- You only need a small, practical subset: one box shape and five arrows.

Interviewers read a lot of designs — a **standard notation** lets them follow yours instantly instead of decoding your personal shorthand.

- Talking through classes in prose is slow and ambiguous; a diagram is fast and precise.
- It forces you to commit: is this inheritance or just "uses"? UML makes you pick the right arrow.
- Even a rough whiteboard sketch using correct symbols reads as senior-level rigor.

A **class diagram** represents one class as a box split into three stacked sections.

- **Top** — the class name.
- **Middle** — attributes (fields), as `name: type`.
- **Bottom** — methods, as `method(params): returnType`.

Each member gets a visibility symbol: `+` public, `-` private, `#` protected.

- `+` public — callable from anywhere.
- `-` private — only inside the class.
- `#` protected — class and its subclasses.

blocks.subTitle: Inheritance
blocks.markdown:
**Inheritance** ('is-a') is drawn as a solid line with a **hollow (unfilled) triangle** arrowhead, pointing from the subclass to its parent.

- `Car --▷ Vehicle` reads "Car is a Vehicle."
- Only one arrow shape means "is-a" in UML — don't reuse the triangle for anything else.

See [inheritance](inheritance).

blocks.subTitle: Association & dependency
blocks.markdown:
Two lighter-weight links for classes that just **know about** or **use** each other.

- **Association** — a plain solid line. One class holds a reference to another as a field, e.g. `Order — Customer`.
- **Dependency** — a **dashed arrow**. One class briefly uses another, e.g. as a method parameter, without storing it.

Dependency is the weakest, most temporary link in UML.

blocks.subTitle: Aggregation vs composition
blocks.markdown:
Both are 'has-a', drawn with a **diamond** at the owner's end — the difference is the diamond's fill and what it means for lifetime.

- **Aggregation** — **hollow diamond**. The part can exist without the whole, e.g. `Team ◇— Player` (a player can exist without a team).
- **Composition** — **filled diamond**. The part's lifetime is tied to the whole, e.g. `House ◆— Room` (a room dies with the house).

See [object-relationships](object-relationships).

blocks.subTitle: Cheat table
blocks.markdown:
One table to hold the whole section.

| Relationship | Arrow |
|---|---|
| Inheritance (is-a) | Solid line, hollow triangle |
| Association (knows-a) | Plain solid line |
| Aggregation (has-a, independent) | Solid line, hollow diamond |
| Composition (has-a, owned) | Solid line, filled diamond |
| Dependency (uses) | Dashed line, open arrow |

**Multiplicity** is a number (or range) written at each end of a relationship line — it states how many instances can be on that side.

- `1` — exactly one. `0..1` — zero or one (optional). `*` (or `0..*`) — zero or more.
- `Order "1" — "*" OrderItem` reads: one Order has many OrderItems, each OrderItem belongs to exactly one Order.
- Getting multiplicity right often matters more to interviewers than the arrow style itself.

A **sequence diagram** shows *behavior over time*: which objects call which methods, in what order — a class diagram can't show that.

- Each object gets a **lifeline** — a vertical dashed line hanging below its box.
- A **message** is a horizontal arrow from one lifeline to another, labeled with the method call.
- Use it sparingly in interviews: only when the interviewer asks "walk me through what happens when...".

What actually matters when you draw live, under time pressure.

- Draw boxes with just **name + 2-3 key attributes/methods** — skip getters/setters, skip full signatures.
- Get the **arrow direction and diamond/triangle choice right**; that's what signals real understanding.
- Multiplicity labels are optional if you're short on time — say them out loud instead.
- A messy but *correctly notated* diagram beats a tidy one with wrong arrows.

blocks.subTitle: Composition vs aggregation on paper
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How do you show composition vs aggregation in UML?**

Both use a diamond at the owning class's end of the line. A **hollow diamond** is aggregation — the part survives without the whole (Team/Player). A **filled diamond** is composition — the part is destroyed with the whole (House/Room). Say the fill out loud too, since it's easy to miss on a whiteboard.

blocks.subTitle: The hollow triangle
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What does a hollow triangle arrowhead mean in UML?**

Inheritance — "is-a". It points from the subclass to the superclass, e.g. Car to Vehicle. It's the only arrow reserved for inheritance, so seeing it should immediately tell you there's a base class and subclasses involved, not just a field reference.

blocks.subTitle: What sequence diagrams are for
blocks.markdown:
**Q: When would you draw a sequence diagram instead of a class diagram?**

When the interviewer wants to see *runtime flow*, not structure — e.g. "walk me through placing an order." A class diagram shows what exists and how classes relate; a sequence diagram shows the actual order of method calls between objects, using lifelines and message arrows.

blocks.subTitle: Reading multiplicity
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What does multiplicity express, and why does it matter?**

It states how many instances sit on each end of a relationship — `1`, `0..1`, or `*`. It matters because it decides real code: `Order "1" — "*" OrderItem` means the Order class likely holds a list of items, not a single reference. Get it wrong and your class fields don't match your diagram.
